payload.question_text: What does speech recognition do? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Reading text aloud is speech synthesis. Recognition moves from speech to text instead.

feedback.intrinsic: No written transcript would be produced.
feedback.instructional: Recognition listens and writes; synthesis speaks.

options.rationale: Recognition takes spoken language as input. It begins with captured speech.
Producing written text from speech is recognition's core role. It is therefore called speech-to-text.
A transcription gives an app usable written content. That supports understanding a spoken request.

payload.explanation: Correct. Recognition listens to speech and produces text.

payload.question_text: What does accessibility mean in a speech-enabled experience?

options.rationale: Accessibility considers people with different abilities and needs. It aims to prevent barriers to use.

options.text: Using one voice for all users
options.rationale: A consistent voice may support branding. It does not address different access needs.
options.better_fit: It fits a consistent brand-voice decision.

feedback.intrinsic: Users could still face access barriers.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility provides usable choices for different needs.

options.rationale: Speech-only input can exclude people who need another method. Accessible applications also provide text alternatives.
options.better_fit: It fits hands-free use for a person who chooses to speak.

feedback.intrinsic: Some users could not use the experience.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility means offering alternatives, not requiring speech.

options.rationale: Sampling rate affects audio detail. It does not by itself remove access barriers.

feedback.intrinsic: Clearer audio would not supply text access.
feedback.instructional: Accessibility concerns user needs and alternative methods.

payload.explanation: Correct. Accessibility designs for different user needs.

payload.question_text: Speech recognition is useful when an application must understand what a person says.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: This would overlook recognition's purpose in a voice interface.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Applications use recognition to turn what people say into usable written text.

payload.explanation: Correct. Recognition makes spoken requests available as text.

payload.question_text: When speech is available, an application no longer needs text-based input and output alternatives.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: This could leave some users without access.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Some users prefer or require non-speech interfaces, so provide text input and output.

payload.explanation: Correct. Speech does not remove the need for text alternatives.

payload.question_text: Which are benefits of speech-enabled experiences? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Speech can reduce reliance on keyboards and screens. This enables hands-free operation.
Speech does not eliminate the need for text alternatives. Some users prefer or require non-speech access.
options.better_fit: Speech-only interaction may fit a limited context, but not accessible general design.

feedback.intrinsic: Users needing text could lose access.
feedback.instructional: Speech expands choices; it should not remove text alternatives.

options.rationale: Speech can be used while another task continues. This supports multitasking.
Speaking and hearing can feel conversational. This can make interactions more natural.

payload.explanation: Correct. Speech can support hands-free work, multitasking, and natural interaction.

options.rationale: Written text can feed synthesis, but it is not the whole scope. Speech capabilities also handle spoken input or output.
options.better_fit: Written text is the input for speech synthesis.

feedback.intrinsic: This would leave out spoken input.
feedback.instructional: Speech capabilities concern spoken language through recognition and synthesis.

options.rationale: Speech capabilities work with spoken language. Recognition and synthesis handle its input or output.
Storing audio does not understand or generate language. It is distinct from speech conversion.
options.better_fit: Audio storage is useful for retaining recordings.

feedback.intrinsic: A recording alone would not create a transcript or reply.
feedback.instructional: Recognition and synthesis perform the language conversions.

options.rationale: Phoneme probabilities can occur inside recognition. They do not describe the complete speech capability.

feedback.intrinsic: This omits usable text and spoken output.
feedback.instructional: Speech capabilities are broader than one internal recognition signal.

payload.explanation: Correct. Speech capabilities work with spoken language.

payload.question_text: Using recognition and synthesis together can enable hands-free operation and support multitasking.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: This overlooks a practical benefit of voice interaction.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition handles spoken input and synthesis provides spoken output.

payload.explanation: Correct. Two-way voice interaction can reduce reliance on keyboards and screens.

payload.question_text: Which name also refers to speech synthesis?

options.rationale: Speech-to-text converts speech into written text. That process is speech recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: A written notice would not be spoken.

options.rationale: Audio capture records incoming sound. It does not generate spoken audio from text.
options.better_fit: It fits the first step of recognition.

options.rationale: Text-to-speech is another name for speech synthesis. Both convert written text into spoken audio.
Language modeling helps select likely word sequences. It is not the text-to-audio capability.

feedback.instructional: Use synthesis when text must be spoken aloud.

payload.question_text: Speech recognition converts written text into spoken audio.

feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition is speech-to-text; synthesis is text-to-speech.

payload.explanation: Correct. That conversion is speech synthesis.

payload.question_text: Speech synthesis listens to spoken language and converts it into written text.

feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Synthesis starts with text and produces spoken audio.

payload.explanation: Correct. That description belongs to speech recognition.

sources.location: sources/4. Introduction to AI speech concepts.md

evidence.statement: The supplied source defines speech recognition as converting spoken words to text and speech synthesis as converting text to spoken audio; the recognition and synthesis items mostly preserve those directions.
Item q6 overgeneralizes by treating spoken language as the sole input or object processed by speech capabilities, although the supplied source states that synthesis starts with written text.

The question in item q6 asks what plural speech capabilities process, but marks only spoken language as correct; the supplied source distinguishes recognition of spoken language from synthesis of written text, making the intended answer insufficiently determinate.
Several distractors reflect credible confusions, such as speech-to-text versus text-to-speech and speech access versus removal of alternatives.

In item q6, options such as only audio storage and only phoneme probabilities are narrow internal or adjacent concepts rather than equally plausible answers to the broad question about speech capabilities.

The artifact explicitly labels and explains realistic misconceptions, including confusing recognition with synthesis, assuming speech removes text alternatives, and confusing audio capture with language conversion.

The ordered session remains almost entirely at Remembering and Understanding levels, with no application or decision task; related concepts are also interleaved rather than building from capability definitions to concrete use cases and implementation choices.

The session uses both multiple choice and true/false, but repeated mechanics occur in blocks: multiple choice at the start, true/false in items 3–4, multiple choice in items 5–6, and true/false again at items 9–10.
Prompt stems vary between what, which, and declarative true/false forms, but several items repeat closely parallel reversal or definition wording, especially the final two true/false items.

All ten items ask for definitions, benefits, or true/false judgments without presenting a credible user task or decision, while the supplied source provides concrete contexts such as customer service, assistants, meetings, healthcare, notifications, and vehicles.

Incorrect options generally include both intrinsic consequences and instructional guidance, such as explaining why removing text alternatives creates access barriers and distinguishing recognition from synthesis.

The Level 1 session appropriately emphasizes foundational recognition, synthesis, accessibility, and user-benefit concepts using Remembering and Understanding tasks; the broad q6 wording adds avoidable difficulty through ambiguity.

Recognition, speech-to-text, synthesis, and text-to-speech are used consistently across most items and align with the supplied source; q6 weakens consistency by describing the two capabilities as if they share only spoken-language processing.

The session is source-faithful and provides clear foundational feedback, but its exact sequence is repetitive, largely recall-based, and lacks the source's authentic application contexts; q6 also introduces a central capability ambiguity.

critical_defects.summary: Item q6 uses a broad plural prompt whose marked answer excludes text input used by speech synthesis.

evidence.statement: The supplied source states that recognition converts spoken words to text while synthesis converts text to spoken audio, so the prompt asking what speech capabilities process does not uniquely support spoken language as the sole correct answer.

largest_gap.summary: The session contains no authentic scenario or decision task despite source material supplying multiple applicable speech use cases.

evidence.statement: All ten prompts are abstract definitions, benefits, or reversals; the supplied source includes concrete customer service, assistant, meeting, healthcare, notification, learning, and vehicle scenarios that are not represented.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Rewrite the prompts and explanations for the two affected existing items as concise source-bounded scenarios involving a credible speech-enabled task, while preserving each item's question_type, answer key, deterministic constraints, and source-faithful concept being tested.

result.concise_summary: The artifact is mostly source-faithful with useful misconception feedback, but q6 is ambiguous and the session lacks authentic scenarios, progression, and stronger mechanic rhythm. Both identified issues are safely repairable within existing item types.

rounds.repair_summary: Rewrote the two affected prompts and explanations as source-bounded customer-service and vehicle scenarios while preserving item order, question types, answer keys, and all unrelated content.

evidence.statement: The source defines recognition as converting spoken words to text and synthesis as converting written text to spoken audio. Most answers match, but q6 marks only “Spoken language” for a broad question about both capabilities, omitting written-text input to synthesis.
The broad wording of q6 makes its single answer incomplete because the source describes both spoken-language input for recognition and written-text input for synthesis.
Distractors such as “Removal of all text interfaces,” “Audio capture,” and “Language modeling” are credible related concepts but are not defensible answers under their item instructions.

Wrong choices diagnose source-grounded misconceptions, including reversing recognition and synthesis, removing accessibility alternatives, confusing audio capture with recognition, and confusing language modeling with synthesis.

The sequence generally moves from definitions to accessibility, scenarios, benefits, combined capabilities, and direction checks, but q6 introduces an overly broad definition after several related items and the final recognition/synthesis checks are repetitive.
The session uses multiple-choice, true/false, and select-all mechanics, but contains adjacent repeated mechanics at the opening and close, including two consecutive true/false items at the end.
Several stems use similar short forms such as “What does,” “What do,” and “Which,” while q9 and q10 repeat nearly identical reversal-check wording.
The customer-service transcription and voice-controlled vehicle scenarios directly match the source’s documented real-world examples and decisions.
Feedback usually identifies the governing conversion or accessibility concept and gives a next-step distinction, such as recognition versus synthesis and speech access versus text alternatives.
The metadata identifies a Level 1 unit with rung 1 remembering items and rung 2 understanding items; definitions, simple scenarios, and direction checks are appropriate for that position.

Recognition, speech-to-text, synthesis, and text-to-speech are used consistently with the source across most items; q6 is the exception because “speech capabilities” is described as processing only spoken language despite synthesis also taking written text.
The artifact is coherent, source-aligned, and accessible for beginners, but q6 creates a scope mismatch and the ending repeats inverse true/false checks, reducing precision and variety.

critical_defects.summary: The broad q6 prompt gives an incomplete source-faithful account of what the two speech capabilities process.

evidence.statement: The source states that recognition converts spoken words into text while synthesis converts written text into spoken audio; q6 asks about speech capabilities broadly but marks only “Spoken language” as correct.

largest_gap.summary: q6’s broad wording makes its sole correct answer incomplete relative to the source’s two capability directions.

evidence.statement: The source distinguishes spoken-language input for recognition from written-text input for synthesis, but q6’s broad stem and answer identify only spoken language.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Change only the question_text to “Which kind of input does speech recognition process?” so the existing correct option “Spoken language” is uniquely aligned with the supplied source. Preserve question_type and all other payload fields.

result.concise_summary: The challenger is mostly source-faithful and suitable for Level 1, with one safe item-level repair needed: narrow q6 so its answer does not misrepresent the scope of speech capabilities.
